Here, we use the double-angle formula for cosine that involves the ${cos}^{2}⁡\theta $ term, given by

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta =2{cos}^{2}⁡\theta -1.
$$

 

Rearranging, we have

$$
{cos}^{2}⁡\theta =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta +1).
$$

Letting $\theta =3x$, we have

$$
{cos}^{2}⁡3x=\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡6x+1).
$$

Substituting this into our integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {cos}^{2}⁡3x\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡6x+1)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{6}\operatorname{sin}⁡6x+\frac{1}{2}x+C \\  & =\frac{1}{12}\operatorname{sin}⁡6x+\frac{x}{2}+C.\end{aligned}
$$
